ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Gastroenterology Referral — Marcus Aurelius — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: New patient visit for chronic epigastric and lower chest pain after meals, poor appetite and poor sleep: cardiac assessment first, review of an opium-containing remedy, and gastroenterology referral for endoscopy

text.paragraph: Chronic burning and pressing pain in the upper abdomen and lower chest after meals for more than a year, with poor appetite, night waking and a 3 kg weight loss, in a 53-year-old man who takes an opium-containing herbal remedy. ECG normal; CT coronary angiography booked for the morning of your appointment. Please perform upper endoscopy with gastric biopsies, find the cause, and advise on treatment. [S]

Urgency: Routine but prompt, within one week. He is stable, with no bleeding, difficulty swallowing or vomiting. No acid-suppressing drug has been started before the endoscopy; he has calcium carbonate as needed. He has been told to call 911 for chest pain at rest lasting more than a few minutes, or with breathlessness, sweating or fainting. [S]

list.item: Is there an esophageal, gastric or duodenal cause for his pain after meals: reflux esophagitis, peptic ulcer, or functional dyspepsia?
Does he have Helicobacter pylori infection?
What treatment do you advise, and for how long?
Could the opium in his remedy be contributing, through slowed stomach emptying or esophageal dysmotility, and does he need manometry or emptying studies?
Does he need repeat endoscopy or other follow-up?

text.paragraph: Burning and pressing pain behind the lower sternum and in the epigastrium about half an hour after meals, mostly after one large late meal, with a sour taste and night waking; never brought on by riding or walking. Poor appetite and a 3 kg weight loss over six months. No NSAIDs or aspirin. Never smoked; wine two or three times a week (AUDIT-C 3). For about six years he has taken an unregulated compounded herbal paste containing opium, about 0.5 g at bedtime most nights, for stomach pain and sleep; prescription drug monitoring shows no controlled prescriptions; a urine drug test today, with his consent, showed morphine and codeine only, consistent with opium, with fentanyl and other drugs negative. He meets one DSM-5-TR criterion (restlessness and poor sleep when he stopped it); no opioid use disorder. Hard stools every two or three days. Chronic insomnia (Insomnia Severity Index 17). PHQ-9 8 with item 9 scored 0; GAD-7 6. Today: weight 63.0 kg (BMI 21.3), blood pressure 124/78, pulse 76; mild epigastric tenderness. ECG normal. Hemoglobin 14.6 g/dL; liver tests and lipase normal; A1c 5.4%; LDL 133 mg/dL; lipoprotein(a) 38 nmol/L. No known allergy [S]

list.item: He has had pain in his chest and stomach after meals for more than a year and wants to know whether his heart is sound. [S]
He sleeps badly and is tired, and must stay clear-headed for his work. [S]
He has taken the herbal paste for years and does not want to be judged for it, or made to stop it before he is ready. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Marcus Aurelius was born at Rome, in a villa on the Caelian Hill, on the sixth day before the Kalends of May (26 April in the Julian calendar) in 121 CE. [D]
He was educated in rhetoric by Fronto, was adopted by the emperor Antoninus Pius in 138 CE, became emperor in 161 CE, at first jointly with Lucius Verus, and ruled alone from 169 CE. [D]

Much of his reign was spent on campaign in central Europe, and the Meditations were probably written there, about 171 to 175 CE; the first book ends 'Among the Quadi at the Granua' and the second 'This in Carnuntum'. [D]

A great pestilence struck the empire during his reign, from 165 CE, spread with the Parthian war and the wars on the Danube; the Life of Marcus says the dead were removed in carts and wagons and that thousands died, many nobles among them. Galen witnessed the epidemic. [D]
The cause of the Antonine Plague is uncertain: Galen's case reports suggest smallpox to many authors, but paleopathological confirmation is lacking. [R]

Cassius Dio, a senator of the period, writes that he was so frail in body that at first he could not endure the cold, that he ate very little and only at night, and that by day he took nothing but the drug called theriac, 'not so much because he feared anything, as because his stomach and chest were in bad condition'. [D]

In the Meditations he thanks the gods that remedies were shown to him in dreams, among them remedies 'against bloodspitting and giddiness', and that his body had held out so long in such a kind of life. [D]

Galen became court physician to the emperors Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus, and prepared his theriac at the court; Marcus Aurelius took theriac daily, to protect against poisons and for his general health. [D]
Theriac was a compound remedy of many ingredients, among them viper's flesh, opium, honey, wine and cinnamon. [D]
Galen relates that the emperor disliked the drowsiness the theriac caused, so the poppy juice was left out; he then could not sleep, and the opium-containing preparation was resumed. [D]

Whether he was dependent on or addicted to opium is disputed. Thomas Africa argued for addiction in 1961; later reviews find no explicit ancient description of opium dependence, call his the one putative case, and favour the most parsimonious reading, that the opium was medicinal rather than hedonic. [R]
As a boy he studied so hard that it impaired his health, which the Life of Marcus calls the only fault to be found in his entire childhood. [D]

About 0.5 g at bedtime most nights; occasionally a second amount in the morning

One or two tablets as needed, at least four hours apart; no more than six a day
Polyethylene glycol 3350 powder, 17 g dissolved in a glass of water by mouth once daily as needed for constipation
Naloxone 4 mg nasal spray, one spray into one nostril for suspected opioid overdose, repeated in 2 to 3 minutes in the other nostril if there is no response; call 911
One spray for suspected overdose; repeat every 2 to 3 minutes if needed

list.item: Burning and pressing pain in the upper abdomen and lower chest after meals, for more than a year and worse over three months, with poor appetite, waking at night with pain and a sour taste, and a 3 kg weight loss; not brought on by exertion; normal ECG; cardiac and peptic causes to be excluded: active, confirmed [S]

Daily use of an unregulated opium-containing herbal remedy for about six years, for stomach pain and sleep; opioid use disorder criteria not met (one DSM-5-TR criterion, restlessness and poor sleep when he stopped it); expected physiological dependence; constipation and possibly slowed gastric emptying from the opioid: active, confirmed [S]
Chronic insomnia disorder for more than a year, with waking from night pain and trouble returning to sleep; Insomnia Severity Index 17 (moderate): active, confirmed [S]
Sustained strain of command: leads a large organization through a long field assignment far from home, with long days and little rest: active, confirmed [S]
Constipation from the opioid in his remedy: hard stools every two or three days: active, confirmed [S]

Cardiac assessment first: twelve-lead ECG today; a structured estimate of the chance of coronary disease; no troponin, because the pain is chronic and there is no acute episode; CT coronary angiography within a week, chosen over stress testing because it excludes both obstructive and non-obstructive plaque and informs the cholesterol decision; call 911 for chest pain at rest lasting more than a few minutes, or pain with breathlessness, sweating or fainting. Guideline: 2021 AHA/ACC/ASE/CHEST/SAEM/SCCT/SCMR Guideline for the Evaluation and Diagnosis of Chest Pain (2021); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, hyperlipidemia and ischemic heart disease monographs (2026) [S]

Respectful review of the opium-containing remedy: what it is, why he takes it, and what it does for him; a DSM-5-TR assessment; a prescription drug monitoring program check; a urine drug test with his consent, explained as part of care; naloxone at home; no alcohol, sleep medicines or other sedatives on the same night; never more than his usual amount; stored closed and out of reach; how opioids slow the gut; no forced or abrupt taper, and any reduction his own choice, made slowly; reviewed at every visit, with the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. Guideline: CDC Clinical Practice Guideline for Prescribing Opioids for Pain, United States, 2022 (2022) [S]

Chronic insomnia: cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) with the clinic's behavioral sleep clinician, six sessions, with a sleep diary, sleep restriction, stimulus control and work on racing thoughts at night; Insomnia Severity Index at intake and at each review; no hypnotic or sedating antihistamine, which would add to the opioid. Guideline: Behavioral and psychological treatments for chronic insomnia disorder in adults: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline (2021); Management of Chronic Insomnia Disorder in Adults: A Clinical Practice Guideline From the American College of Physicians (2016) [S]

Strain of command and mood: PHQ-9 and GAD-7 at intake and at follow-up; protected time for meals and sleep, decisions delegated after a set hour, and his evening writing kept; counselling if scores rise. Guideline: Depression and Suicide Risk in Adults: Screening (2023) [S]

Constipation: polyethylene glycol as needed, fluids and fiber; review as the remedy changes. Guideline: CDC Clinical Practice Guideline for Prescribing Opioids for Pain, United States, 2022 (2022) [S]
Referral to gastroenterology, Felix Brandt-Oyelaran, MD, ordered 0174-05-12 [S]
